title: The forest years
hookLine: life in Chitrakoot and among the forest sages; the four stages of life
carry: four stages of life, each with its own dharma

lines: BARK, FRUIT, A RIVER AT DAWN.
cards: Start with what they left. A prince who grew up with servants and elephants. A princess who wore silk.
A brother who rode in chariots beside him. Now: a hut of leaves and branches that Lakshmana built by hand, on a hill called Chitrakoot, beside a river.
They wear bark cloth, eat fruit and roots, and bathe in the river at dawn. Rama points out the trees and birds to Sita, the flowers on the hillside, the elephants coming down to drink.
For a while, this is the whole story. No battles. No palace.

teach.b: After Bharata's visit they move deeper south, into the great Dandaka forest, and meet the sages who live in the woods.
The sage Atri and his wife Anasuya, a holy woman well-known for her devotion, who welcomes Sita like a daughter and gives her gifts and advice. The sage Agastya, who gives Rama divine weapons.

The text says they spent about ten years moving from one hermitage to another, learning, listening, living simply. Eventually they settle at Panchavati, by the Godavari river. Today's word: vanaprastha.
Vana means forest; vanaprastha is the one who goes to the forest. It's one of the four stages of life in Hindu tradition.

First, the student. Second, the householder: work, family, raising children, giving. Third, vanaprastha: when your children have children, you step back from the business of the world and turn toward God.
Fourth, the renouncer, who lets go of everything. Rama is too young for the forest stage; he's there by exile, not by age. But those years look a lot like it.
Fewer things, fewer roles, more attention. Here's the teaching: Hinduism doesn't ask everyone to do everything at once.

teach.h: FOUR STAGES OF LIFE, EACH WITH ITS OWN DHARMA.
teach.b: Each stage of life has its own dharma, its own right work. A student's job isn't a grandparent's.
Many Hindu grandparents still live a version of the third stage today, with more prayer, more pilgrimage, and handing things on.

how: Hindu tradition describes four stages of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer); today some older Hindus take up a simpler, more devotional life in the spirit of vanaprastha, and Chitrakoot and Panchavati are pilgrimage places.

o: a hermit who has given up every tie for good
the forest stage of life, stepping back to turn inward
a pilgrimage made to a sacred forest shrine

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: the hill with the leaf hut

s: vanaprastha is the first stage of life
it's the third: after student and householder, before renouncer.
Rama goes to the forest at the traditional age for vanaprastha
he's young, there by exile; his years just resemble it.
the text says they spent years among the forest sages
about ten years moving from hermitage to hermitage.

games.q: you're Sita, a princess now living in a hut of leaves for fourteen years. how do you live it?
o: count the days until the palace.
learn the forest, and from the sages who live in it.
ask to go back to your father's kingdom.
games.why: in the text the three are happy there, and Sita learns from holy women like Anasuya.

practice: Put your phone face down and sit with nothing in your hands, like the three at Chitrakoot. Ask which stage of life you're in: learning, building, or letting go. What's the right work of this stage, and what belongs to a later one?
If you pray, offer this stage of your life to God. If not, simply name it, and sit with it.

wordCard.voice: Vanaprastha. The forest-dweller: the third stage of life, when you step back from the world and turn inward.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one who goes out to the forest (vana), the third stage of life.

carryVoice: Your line: four stages of life, each with its own dharma. A hut of leaves showed the third one early. Day forty-five, done.
